correctness.rationale: The Fourier transform is invertible in nonmodular characteristic. The proof directly derives the binomial coordinate equations, establishes full signed-doubling support and inverse-paired squaring, and proves the finite-field descent condition on Frobenius orbits. Each common-root count is the claimed gcd and is prime to the coefficient characteristic; Möbius inversion counts free L-orbits. Existence follows by Fourier inversion. A standalone direct multiplication verifier exhausts 17 small cyclic cases and C3×C3 over F2. Size-17 numerical checks are only formula evaluations, not exhaustive proofs.

originality.rationale: The 2026 Alexander-quandle Fourier paper establishes the character equation and integral rigidity; a preexisting characteristic-zero orbit decomposition classifies complex points. Neither supplies the finite-field Galois merging of signed-doubling orbits and gcd root restrictions for all odd-order finite abelian groups. Direct same-object comparisons include the arithmetic changes 68 versus 24 on C11 and 648 versus 36 on C17. published-finding corpus searches found related modular idempotent work but no dominating nonmodular general formula. Complete global novelty is not certified.
residual_risks: Kaur–Singh, Decomposition of quandle rings of Takasaki quandles (arxiv:2303.06948), was accessible only as an abstract specifying real/complex coefficients; its full text was not inspected and possible indirect reduction remains a risk.
A general preexisting classification of finite-field rational points of binomial monomial systems might subsume this special case.
Search coverage cannot guarantee global novelty or priority; the exact field-descent formula has not undergone independent bibliographic review.

value.rationale: Idempotent elements of quandle algebras motivate knot/link-coloring enhancements. The exact all-field rational-point census and nontrivial Fourier-support enumerator are intrinsic arithmetic invariants across every odd-order finite abelian core quandle. Frobenius orbit fusion and root restrictions vary with the coefficient field and produce demonstrably distinct counts for the same quandle, not a routine restatement of its complex-field orbit decomposition.
